Regulatory Update
- Regional Director, South Western Region, MCA rejected the amalgamation scheme

Management Response
- Company is evaluating its next course of action
- Can refile under Section 233 or pursue approval under Section 232
- Company states no material impact on business operations

Key Takeaway
- Internal restructuring faces regulatory delays
- Further approvals and compliance requirements remain
- Impact: Negative

SEBI EXTENDS IPO ISSUE-SIZE RELAXATION DEADLINE TO MARCH 31, 2027

• SEBI extends the relaxation allowing companies to revise IPO issue sizes by up to 50% without filing a fresh Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP).

• New deadline extended to March 31, 2027, from the earlier September 30, 2026.

• Previously, IPO issue-size revisions exceeding 20% required companies to file fresh draft offer documents.

• SEBI had increased the permissible revision limit to 50% in April 2026 to provide flexibility amid geopolitical tensions and challenging capital-raising conditions.

• Extension allows IPO-bound companies greater flexibility to adjust issue sizes according to market conditions without restarting the entire draft filing process.

• Move could reduce regulatory delays and help companies proceed with planned public offerings.

Impact: Positive — Greater flexibility in IPO sizing could support fundraising activity, reduce compliance-related delays and benefit companies preparing to enter the primary market.

PAYTM: NPCI DEFERS MDR IMPLEMENTATION ON SELECT P2M UPI TRANSACTIONS UNTIL AFTER DIWALI

• NPCI has decided to postpone the implementation of Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on select Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI transactions.

• Earlier, NPCI had issued a circular dated September 15, 2026, regarding the levy of MDR on select P2M transactions.

• Revised implementation will take place after Diwali, with the effective date to be announced separately.

• Decision comes ahead of the festive season, providing additional time for merchants and payment service providers to prepare.

• Paytm disclosed the development to stock exchanges on October 13, 2026.

Impact: Mixed — The postponement delays potential MDR-linked revenue opportunities for payment service providers, including Paytm, but provides more time for implementation and reduces immediate cost pressure on affected merchants.

China's solar cell exports to India have fallen by a massive 98% in just one year. China's solar cell exports to India declined from 2.68 GW in August 2025 to just 0.07 GW in August 2026!

This is quite an extraordinary development!

The big reason? India's ALMM List-II policy, which came into effect on June 1, 2026.

Look at how India's solar manufacturing ecosystem is shaping up:

Solar module manufacturing capacity: 217 GW
Domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity: 39.4 GW
Chinese solar cell exports to India: Down 98% YoY in August

This is a compelling example of how government policy can reshape an entire industry's supply chain.

But there is another side to this story.

India has built massive solar module capacity, but domestic cell manufacturing still needs to catch up.

Further upstream, we still depend on China for wafers and polysilicon.

The next big opportunity lies in building the entire solar manufacturing value chain in India, not just assembling modules. And that is indeed taking place

POLYCAB INDIA: MSCI INDEX DELETION LIKELY, SAYS MOTILAL OSWAL 🔴

• Motilal Oswal flags potential removal of Polycab India from MSCI indices under MSCI's insolvency-related eligibility rules.

• MSCI policy covers securities under Enhanced Surveillance Measure (ESM) and Insolvency Resolution Process frameworks.

• Securities placed on the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (IAB) list are excluded from the MSCI Equity Universe.

• Existing MSCI constituents entering the IAB list are deleted on the last business day of the month, with at least two full business days' notice.

• Such securities cannot be reintroduced into MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes for 12 months following deletion.

• Potential deletion could trigger selling pressure from passive funds tracking MSCI indices.

Impact: Negative 🔴 — Potential MSCI exclusion could lead to passive fund outflows and near-term pressure on Polycab shares. However, the deletion remains an expectation, not a confirmed MSCI announcement.

MORGAN STANLEY ON INDIA HEALTHCARE

Supreme Court questioned why drug price controls currently cover only oncology treatments.

The government informed the court that it has approved a 30% trade margin cap specifically on cancer drugs.

The court also questioned the practice of letting manufacturers set their own drug prices, while the government urged balancing affordability with drug availability.

The next hearing is scheduled for October 27, with the latest observations viewed as incrementally negative.

Expanding pricing controls beyond oncology would raise regulatory uncertainty, though a measured government approach remains possible.

D Structural drivers such as low bed density and the ongoing need for private capacity continue to underpin the long-term positive view on the healthcare sector.

Demeter Advisors’ Ashwini Agarwal sees attractive valuations in IT services, with large-cap stocks offering better value than small-caps. He also sees opportunities in select SMID-cap IT companies, while banking sector growth is likely to remain subdued

India now makes some of cheapest solar power in world. Making one megawatt hour of solar electricity costs about $35 in India, versus $44 on global average

When companies sign solar contracts, price stays locked for 25 years. Coal electricity gets more expensive every year because fuel prices rise with inflation. Every year that passes, gap between solar and coal grows wider. 

India used to avoid heavy industry because power was too costly that problem no longer exists because of how cheap solar has become

Europe started charging extra money on steel and aluminum imports based on how much carbon was used to make them. Indian steel now costs 20 to 35% more when sold to Europe because of this tax. 

But India makes green hydrogen cheaply because solar power is very affordable. Research from Berkeley shows India can produce green steel cheaper than coal steel by 2030. Companies using coal pay full carbon tax. Companies using green energy skip it. India cost disadvantage is turning into cost advantage.

Setting up data centers in India costs 30 to 50% less than in US or Europe. Building one megawatt of data center capacity costs $6 to 7 million in India, compared to $10 to 14 million in Western countries. 

Chennai electricity costs less than half of what Singapore charges. India data center capacity is expected to grow from 1.5 gigawatts to 12 gigawatts by 2030. Cheap power is doing what government subsidies could not do for decades, it is pulling big tech investment into India

I would say, if you read the filings of companies over the last year, you will notice that many are entering into renewable energy partnerships, which are helping them reduce their power costs. This is one way Indian industries are getting access to cheaper electricity.

Right now, India is importing batteries from China, and every month we are seeing tons of new BESS orders. Just think about what could happen over the next 5 years when India slowly starts building its own battery manufacturing capacity. 

That could change the entire dynamics of the energy sector. As renewable energy and battery storage become more affordable, the cost of electricity could come down further, making Indian industries more competitive in the long run.

Anandrathi IC on Jyoti CNC | Channel Check Update - AC & Cement

> *Jyoti CNC* *: Initiating Coverage with BUY, TP of Rs. 1,275* 

 Jyoti CNC is well-positioned to capitalise on a multi-year capex upcycle across Aerospace & Defence, Auto, General Engineering and EMS, driving sustained demand for CNC machines. 

The recent *capacity expansion to ~16,000 machines from 6,000 machines unlocks revenue potential of ~Rs. 60bn* , while a healthy *order book of Rs. 48.5bn* provides 18–20 months of revenue visibility. We expect revenue CAGR of *25–30% over FY26–29E* , with *EBITDA margins sustaining at 25–27%* , supported by operating leverage, favourable product mix and increasing localisation.

We initiate coverage with a *BUY rating and a target price of Rs. 1,275,* valuing the company at *~40x TTM Sep-28E P/E, at a 20% premium* to the BSE Capital Goods sector’s 2-year forward multiple, reflecting its superior growth profile.

> AC Channel Check Update

Our channel checks show room-AC *demand recovered strongly in July–August after a weak May–June* , held up well in September with *comfortable channel inventory* , and *dealers now expect a festive pickup* once Pitru Paksh ends. *LG and Blue Star raised prices again from 1 October to offset higher commodity costs.* Voltas remains the preferred mass-market brand, ahead of Blue Star and LG, while Daikin leads the premium segment, followed by O-General and Panasonic. *Mass brands are pushing hard with festive discounts, bank-linked cashback (LG up to 26%) and no-cost EMI schemes,* which should cushion the price hikes and support premiumisation, and e-commerce’s share has risen structurally above 15%. *We stay positive on the sector given the strong Q2FY27 recovery and healthy festive momentum* , but expect margins to stay under pressure despite repeated price hikes.

> Cement Channel Check Update

Our cement channel checks show companies have announced *price hikes of about Rs10–15/bag* across regions in October 2026 to partly pass on elevated input and fuel costs, and dealers expect them to hold, helped by *post-monsoon demand recovery and festive-season construction* . Sustenance will be uneven, though: firm housing, infrastructure and real-estate demand should support prices in the *South (Hyderabad, Bangalore), North (Jaipur, Delhi) and West (Mumbai), with non-trade hikes of up to Rs20/bag* , while Chennai saw only a billing increase and a slowdown in government-funded projects. In the *Central region (Indore, Agra, Lucknow) and Nagpur, soft demand makes the Rs10/bag* hikes harder to sustain. The *East remains weakest* : Kolkata rolled back its September hike amid stalled construction and the long Durga Puja break, and Patna’s hike failed due to an extended monsoon and stiff competition. Overall, the ability to pass on rising fuel costs through higher prices will be key to protecting margins.

PLASTIBLENDS INDIA Q2 : REVENUE GROWTH DESPITE HIGH RAW MATERIAL & ENERGY COSTS

• Company reported revenue growth despite challenging market conditions, supported by improved price realisations.

• Raw Material & Operating Costs: Elevated raw material prices, power and freight expenses continued to pressure profitability.

• Gujarat Power Costs: Fuel surcharge increased significantly during Q2, further raising manufacturing costs.

• Margin Outlook: Company absorbed part of the higher costs to protect customers and market share. Management plans to pass these costs on in subsequent quarters.

• Exports: Export business performed well, supported by entry into new markets and an improved product mix.

• Rupee Depreciation: INR weakened to approximately ₹96/USD from ₹88/USD a year ago, improving export competitiveness but increasing import costs.

• Engineering Plastics: Division continues to grow, with management expecting strong momentum ahead.

• Solar Expansion: Commissioned a 5.2 MW solar open-access power project in Gujarat in September 2026 to help offset higher energy costs.

• Management Outlook: Focus remains on cost optimisation, operational efficiency, export growth and sustainable expansion.

GOKALDAS EXPORTS LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Contract apparel manufacturer serving global fashion brands.
- Major markets include the US and Europe.
- India operations manufacture woven and knitted garments.
- Africa operations operate through subsidiary Atraco.
- Atraco operates four factories in Kenya and one in Ethiopia.
- Africa exports benefit from AGOA tariff access.
- BTPL operates a knit fabric processing mill in Tamil Nadu.

Africa Business Growth
- FY27 revenue target: US$115–120 million.
- FY26 Africa revenue stood at approximately US$80 million.
- H2 FY27 EBITDA margin guidance: 8–10%.
- Recovery depends on higher volumes and AGOA tariff access.
- AGOA restoration currently extends through December 2026.

BTPL Merger & Margin Improvement
- Merger completion targeted for Q3 FY27.
- FY27 revenue guidance: Above ₹1,000 Cr.
- EBITDA profitability targeted for H2 FY27.
- FY28 EBITDA margin target: 12%.
- Merger requires NCLT approval.
- Profitability depends on improving from Q4 FY26's 4–5% EBITDA loss.

India Capacity Expansion
- Bhopal second unit has 1,000 machines.
- Full utilisation targeted by Q3 FY27.
- Karnataka Kolar Gold Fields unit targets utilisation by Q1–Q2 FY27.
- Combined steady-state annual revenue potential: ₹300 Cr.
- Capacity ramp-up should support India revenue growth.

New Customer Wins
- Four new premium customers signed for India operations.
- Two additional premium customers signed for Africa operations.
- New customers include US and European brands.
- Revenue contribution expected to begin in FY27.
- New customers could contribute around 5% of revenue initially.
- Contributions are expected to scale over time.

Financial Estimates
| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue (₹ Cr) | 5,210 | 6,503 | 7,289 |
| Revenue Growth | 28.2% | 24.8% | 12.1% |
| PAT (₹ Cr) | 212 | 299 | 382 |
| PAT Growth | 112.2% | 40.8% | 27.6% |
| Forward P/E | 26.9x | 19.1x | 15.0x |

Key Risks
- Africa growth depends on AGOA renewal beyond December 2026.
- FY26 Africa revenue fell 19% after AGOA lapsed.
- The disruption cost approximately ₹180 Cr.
- Kenya's 10% tariff assumption must hold.
- US tariff rates above 20% could pressure margins.
- FY26 absorbed ₹90 Cr in net tariff discounts.
- BTPL's turnaround depends on merger approval and execution.
- India capacity ramp-up must meet utilisation targets.

Key Takeaway
- Africa recovery and India capacity expansion support FY27 growth.
- BTPL integration offers additional revenue and margin potential.
- New premium customers could diversify the customer base.
- Tariff policy and AGOA continuity remain major uncertainties.
- Merger execution and capacity utilisation are key monitorables.

RELIGARE ENTERPRISES LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Core Investment Company with a diversified financial services portfolio.
- Holds 63.2% of Care Health Insurance.
- Care contributed approximately 94% of consolidated FY26 revenue.
- Owns 100% of Religare Broking and Religare Finvest.
- Religare Finvest holds 87.5% of Religare Housing Finance.
- Care operates retail and group health insurance across 40+ products.
- Broking offers equity, derivatives, commodities and currency trading.
- Finvest is rebuilding its secured-led MSME lending platform.
- Housing Finance provides small-ticket home loans and LAP.

Proposed Demerger & Restructuring
- February 2026 board-approved scheme proposes business transfers to Religare Finvest.
- Lending, broking and ancillary financial services are proposed for transfer.
- Religare Enterprises would become a pure-play health insurance holding company.
- Completion target: 15–18 months from February 2026.
- Religare Finvest listing is targeted for Q1 FY28.
- NCLT, shareholder, creditor and regulatory approvals remain pending.
- The RBI did not approve the scheme in mid-2026.

Care Health Insurance
- Management targets Ind AS combined ratio near 100% within two years.
- Premium growth guidance: 18–24% annually.
- Operating scale is expected to support underwriting improvement.
- Medical inflation and competitive group pricing remain challenges.
- Promoter look-through stake in Care is approximately 18–19%.
- This remains below the cited IRDA promoter threshold of 25–26%.
- No committed timeline exists to close the ownership gap.

Religare Housing Finance
- Profitability targeted within 12–18 months from mid-2026.
- ₹250 Cr capital earmarked from the ₹1,500 Cr warrant issue.
- FY26 loss stood at ₹18.6 Cr on ₹30 Cr income.
- Current monthly disbursements remain below ₹10 Cr.
- Profitability depends on scaling secured lending disbursements.

Religare Broking
- Client debit book grew 75% YoY in Q4 FY26.
- Quarterly interest income increased 44%.
- FY26 non-broking income base stood at ₹373 Cr.
- Margin funding and third-party distribution are key growth initiatives.
- Diversification aims to expand recurring non-broking revenue.

Religare Finvest
- New lending expected to commence within the next few quarters.
- New CEO: Karthik Srinivasan.
- Available cash: ₹591 Cr.
- Tangible net worth: ₹915 Cr.
- Lending recovery remains at an early stage.
- Residual SME book stands at approximately ₹60 Cr.
- No dated disbursement targets have been provided.

Financial Estimates
| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue (₹ Cr) | 10,463 | 12,752 | 15,316 |
| Revenue Growth | 23.2% | 21.9% | 20.1% |
| PAT (₹ Cr) | 164 | 786 | 1,128 |
| PAT Growth | 124.8% | 377.7% | 43.6% |
| Forward P/E | 81.4x | 16.8x | 11.1x |

Key Risks
- Demerger completion remains uncertain after the RBI's response.
- Care's promoter ownership gap limits restructuring flexibility.
- Housing Finance profitability depends on substantial disbursement growth.
- Finvest's new lending platform has yet to scale.
- Care's combined ratio target depends on premium growth and claims control.
- ₹750 Cr Lakshmi Vilas Bank deposit recovery remains unresolved.
- ESOP and preference-share litigation remain open.
- SEBI show-cause notice remains a legal overhang.

Key Takeaway
- Care Health Insurance remains the core earnings driver.
- Demerger could simplify the group structure and unlock value.
- Broking and lending offer additional growth opportunities.
- Regulatory approvals and lending execution remain critical.
- Legal disputes and ownership constraints could sustain the holding-company discount.

SUMITOMO CHEMICAL INDIA LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Manufactures and markets crop protection products.
- Portfolio includes insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and biologicals.
- Also offers plant growth regulators and fumigants.
- Domestic distribution network includes 15,000+ dealers.
- Exports include contract manufacturing for Sumitomo Chemical Company, Japan.
- Operates five plants across Gujarat, Maharashtra and Silvassa.

Dahej Greenfield Expansion
- Planned investment: ₹500–600 Cr over five years.
- Projects cover all seven approved products.
- First ₹150 Cr project targets commercialisation within two years.
- Export CRAMS revenue currently stands at ₹100–150 Cr.
- Expansion aims to increase export manufacturing revenue.
- Timely product approvals remain critical for scale-up.

Bhavnagar Capacity Expansion
- ₹55 Cr investment to double capacity for an SCC-invented molecule.
- Completion targeted by Q4 FY27.
- SCIL aims to meet 40–50% of global requirements.
- Incremental export revenue expected from FY28.

Tarapur Manufacturing Expansion
- INDIFLIN technical manufacturing line targeted for completion by March 2027.
- Enables 100% of domestic Excalia Max demand to be met locally.
- This would eliminate imports from Japan for domestic requirements.

Specialty Product Growth
- Excalia Max and Lentigo exceeded FY26 internal targets.
- Management expects continued growth across Kharif and Rabi seasons.
- These products could support specialty revenue growth in FY27.
- Performance remains sensitive to weather conditions.

Profitability & Margins
- FY26 EBITDA margin reached a record 20.7%.
- Sustaining margins above 20% depends on cost control.
- Further cost inflation may require price increases.
- Successful cost pass-through is important for profitability.

Key Risks
- Dahej revenue depends on timely approvals for seven products.
- Excalia Max and Lentigo growth could face weather disruptions.
- Specialty product growth requires sustained seasonal demand.
- Input-cost inflation could pressure margins if pricing adjustments lag.

Key Takeaway
- Dahej, Bhavnagar and Tarapur offer manufacturing growth opportunities.
- Export CRAMS and specialty products could support revenue expansion.
- Local production may reduce dependence on imports from Japan.
- Product approvals, weather and margin sustainability remain key monitorables.

THE NEW INDIA ASSURANCE COMPANY LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW

Business Overview
- India's largest non-life insurer by gross direct premium.
- Offers health, fire, motor, marine, liability, aviation and crop insurance.
- Health and personal accident contribute 48.16% of premiums.
- Fire contributes 15.52% of premiums.
- Motor third-party contributes 13.04% of premiums.
- Government-owned insurer with operations across India and 24 countries.
- Designated a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer (D-SII).

Combined Ratio Improvement
- FY26 internal target: Around 113% combined ratio.
- Q1 FY26 combined ratio stood at 116.16%.
- Management targets approximately 3% improvement during FY26.
- Lower combined ratios could reduce underwriting losses.
- Better underwriting performance could improve return on equity.

Health Insurance Profitability
- Overall health loss ratio target: 98–100%.
- Q3 FY26 health ICR improved from 103% to 91%.
- Health represents 48.16% of total premiums.
- Sustained improvement could materially support combined ratio reduction.
- Retail health pricing remains constrained by IRDAI regulations.

ROE & New Opportunities
- Nine-month FY26 ROE stood at 4.95%.
- Management targets double-digit ROE.
- Lower incurred claim ratios are the primary improvement lever.
- Parametric insurance is gaining traction.
- Around 10–12 parametric insurance contracts have been completed.

Key Risks
- Motor TP premiums have not been revised since 2022.
- Motor TP ICR stood at 108.2% in FY25.
- Retail health premium increases are capped at 10% annually.
- Medical inflation remains elevated at 14–15%.
- Air India aviation claim pushed aviation ICR to 323% for 9M FY26.
- Marine ship-sinking claims raised marine ICR to 119% in Q3 FY26.
- Wage revision arrears of approximately ₹2,500 Cr affected FY26.
- Additional family pension costs of ₹700–800 Cr were expected in Q4 FY26.
- These costs could increase the expense ratio.

Key Takeaway
- Health claims improvement is central to profitability recovery.
- Combined ratio reduction is critical for achieving double-digit ROE.
- Motor TP pricing and medical inflation remain structural challenges.
- Large claims and employee-related costs could create earnings volatility.

WELSPUN CORP LIMITED – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Manufactures large-diameter welded pipes for oil, gas, water and emerging energy applications.
- Operates pipe manufacturing facilities in India, the USA and Saudi Arabia.
- Holds over 33% of the US line pipe market.
- Welspun Flow manufactures ductile iron pipes for water distribution.
- WSSL produces stainless steel bars and seamless pipes.
- Sintex manufactures water storage tanks and plastic pipes.
- Welspun Shield manufactures TMT rebars.
- FY26 consolidated revenue: ₹16,770 Cr.
- Order book: ₹25,350–25,750 Cr, booked through FY28.

Growth Targets & Expansion
- FY28 revenue target: ₹20,000 Cr.
- FY28 EBITDA target: ₹2,850 Cr.
- US LSAW plant adds 300 KMTPA capacity.
- Saudi LSAW plant adds 350 KMTPA capacity.
- Saudi DI pipe plant adds 250 KMTPA capacity.
- All three plants targeted to become operational by FY27-end.
- US order book stands at approximately ₹25,750 Cr, or $2.7 billion.
- US order visibility extends through FY28.
- Little Rock plant qualification could unlock FY29 orders.
- Saudi DI plant could replace imports with local supply.
- Management expects around two-thirds of import-served Saudi DI demand to shift locally.

Financial Estimates
| Metric | FY27E | FY28E | FY29E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue (₹ Cr) | 20,000 | 23,500 | 26,500 |
| Revenue Growth | 19.3% | 17.5% | 12.8% |
| PAT (₹ Cr) | 1,950 | 2,338 | 2,707 |
| PAT Growth | 20.9% | 19.9% | 15.8% |
| Forward P/E | 35.1x | 29.3x | 25.3x |

Key Risks
- Delays in commissioning could push full-volume contributions into FY29.
- Saudi competition from Jindal Saw, Man Industries and Ratnamani may pressure pricing.
- Indian DI pipe demand remains exposed to JJM funding delays.
- Industry overcapacity could force Anjar toward lower-margin pig iron exports.
- Sintex continues incurring losses while building distribution.
- Water-sector demand recovery may take longer than expected.

Key Takeaway
- New US and Saudi capacity supports the next growth phase.
- US order visibility provides revenue coverage through FY28.
- Saudi DI localisation offers import-substitution opportunities.
- Commissioning timelines, pricing pressure and water-sector weakness remain key risks.

KALYANI STEELS LIMITED – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Manufactures forging and engineering-grade carbon and alloy steel.
- Operates an integrated 250,000 MT annual-capacity plant at Ginigera, Karnataka.
- Plant operations are handled by Hospet Steels Limited, a JV with Mukand Limited.
- Manufacturing contributed 97% of FY26 turnover.
- Rolled products generated ₹15,657 million in FY26.
- Bharat Forge and Kalyani Technoforge together contributed 48% of FY26 sales.

Growth Targets & Expansion
- FY28 related-party sales target: ₹13,500 million.
- Bharat Forge supply target: ₹6,500 million in FY28.
- Kalyani Technoforge supply target: ₹7,000 million in FY28.
- Combined target equals approximately 73% of FY26 revenue from operations.
- Approved single-source supplier status supports OEM-linked demand.
- KTFL target rises from ₹4,058.83 million in FY26.
- Merger of Kalyani Transmission Technologies into KTFL consolidated demand from April 1, 2024.
- Bharat Forge provided a ₹470 million trade advance.
- Advance tenure does not exceed 365 days, supporting working capital and order visibility.

Capacity & Operational Considerations
- The 250,000 MT plant is operating near full capacity.
- Higher related-party sales may require reallocating existing customer volumes.
- Alternatively, additional capacity may be needed to support projected demand.
- No specific capacity expansion plan has been outlined.

Key Risks
- Customer concentration could increase significantly under FY28 targets.
- Bharat Forge and KTFL could represent 73% of FY26 revenue from operations.
- Rising import-dependent coking coal costs could pressure margins.
- Coking coal declined from $254/MT in CY24 to $206/MT in CY25.
- Governance concerns remain following a February 2026 SEBI settlement order.
- A temporary shortfall in independent director requirements adds governance risk.
- Dependence on Hospet Steels and its Mukand JV creates operational exposure.

Key Takeaway
- Growth visibility depends heavily on Bharat Forge and KTFL demand.
- Near-full capacity limits the ability to absorb incremental volumes.
- Customer concentration, raw material costs and governance require close monitoring.

NUVAMA WEALTH MANAGEMENT LTD – BUSINESS OVERVIEW & GROWTH OUTLOOK

Business Overview
- Operates an integrated wealth and financial services platform.
- Wealth Management serves affluent, HNI and ultra-HNI clients.
- Products include mutual funds, AIFs, PMS, fixed income and insurance.

What regulators see that investors often ignore 👇

Every time a regulator acts, investors first ask: "How much EPS gets hit?" Regulators ask something else: "Is the market structure fair for the end consumer?" That's a very different lens. 
Thoughts on recent #PBFintech & older #IEX n more

Case in point: Recent change on insurance commissions. The proposed changes effectively aim to reduce distribution costs & curb excessive upfront payouts on some products. Investors see lower margins. Regulators see lower customer acquisition costs & better value for policyholders.

Truth is, hardly anyone argues that insurance has zero mis-selling. Higher upfront commissions have often created incentives to sell what pays the most, not what suits the customer best. If that problem exists, intervention shouldn't be surprising.

The irony is that many investors celebrate efficiency in every industry except their own portfolio holdings. When a regulator targets excess distribution costs, the reaction is often outrage instead of introspection.

Look at insurance expense ratios. Even as the industry scaled up, commission/expense pools as a % of premium remained elevated in several segments. The regulator's job is to ask: why isn't scale translating into lower customer costs?

Learning from MFs TER. Every TER cut was seen as fatal attack. Prediction was: growth will die, distributors will vanish, profit collapse. Instead industry adapted. Players became efficient, direct plans gained share, technology reduced costs, investor participation & AUM surged

Market coupling in power exch. Investors focus: which exchange lose market share. Regulators focus: consumers get better price discovery. Market coupling means bids/orders from all exch get pooled to discover a single price. One price improves efficiency & reduces fragmentation

Could one exchange lose moat? Maybe. But from system perspective, better price discovery, deeper liquidity & lower market distortion are hard to ignore.
Regulators rarely optimize for shareholder returns. They optimize for consumers, market efficiency & long-term public interest

Think about hospitals. If tomorrow there is stricter price regulation, hospital stocks may get hit. As investors we'd feel the pain. But can anyone honestly deny healthcare costs are becoming unaffordable for a large section of Indians?
One may argue India's healthcare is still cheaper than many countries. True. But the person comparing prices globally is not the same person struggling to pay a hospital bill locally.

Markets often assume regulators must protect industry profitability. Regulators believe industries shouldn't fleece poor customers. When public benefit & industry profits collide, the regulator's choice is usually obvious.

That's why stock market reaction is often the last variable in the regulator's decision. If a policy improves consumer outcomes, transparency, affordability or efficiency, temporary shareholder pain rarely changes the outcome.

30 yrs ago it was Ratan Tata vs Russi Mody. Today, many see shades of that battle in the Chandra vs Noel Tata face-off
Back in the 1990s, Ratan Tata was consolidating authority within a sprawling Tata empire run by powerful Operating entity heads. Russi Mody was among the most influential Tata executives of his era. Larger-than-life personality, huge public profile & massive influence within the group.
Ratan Tata believed Tata Group needed one strategic centre of gravity. Not multiple power centres running individual fiefdoms. Eventually, Russi Mody exited & Ratan Tata tightened control over the conglomerate.
Fast forward three decades.
The debate is again centred around leadership, control & the future direction of Tata Sons. This time its Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, & N Chandrasekaran, who leads Tata Sons
Key contentions are Chandra’s reappointment as chairman & Tata Sons listing. Noel Tata has opposed both
The striking part? Tata Sons board backed Chandra by a 4:1 vote, while Noel Tata stood opposed
Russi Mody took the battle public. Media interviews, public sparring & headline-grabbing exchanges became part of the story.
Chandra, however, has largely stayed silent in public
Whether history repeats or merely echoes, one thing is clear
Generational change of Tata leadership eventually confronts the same question.

Is India investing enough for future capacity

India is usually described as a consumption economy. Consumption contributes >60% of GDP. But the story becomes incomplete when we ignore what's happening on the investment side and other aspects of our economy

India's Gross Capital Formation is ~32.6% of GDP. Lower than China's ~40%, but China's per capita GDP is several times of India's. Comparing ratios without considering income levels misses the context.

A developing country cannot allocate every ₹ toward factories & infra. A large share of resources must also support the bottom of the pyramid through housing, healthcare, education & welfare.

A harmonious society requires a minimum standard of living for those at the bottom. India is building capacity while simultaneously funding social stability. That's a tougher balancing act than many realize.

So let's move beyond GDP narratives & look at hard physical data. India's share of global GDP is only ~3.5% yet produces roughly 10% of the world's steel. Steel almost 3x our weight in global GDP. Steel isn't consumed for consumption's sake, but goes into factories, rail tracks, power plants, ports, airports, infrastructure etc

Cement tells the same story. India produces ~400 MT annually out of ~4,000 MT globally. Again, roughly 10% global share despite only ~3.5% share of world GDP. Countries don't consume steel & cement at this scale unless they are building physical assets. These are the raw materials of future GDP.

Power generation presents a slightly different picture. India's share of global electricity output is lower than steel & cement, but still materially ahead of its global GDP share. India with 1800bn units vs 32,000bn units, 6% global share

The evidence suggests India is investing for future capability. One may argue the investment cycle started later than it should have, but the direction is unmistakable. Steel, Cement & Power share point toward economy preparing for a much larger future.

The scale of projects are also changing. DFCs, industrial corridors, semiconductor fabs, renewable energy parks, metros, airports, transmission corridors & logistics networks are larger than anything India attempted before.

If this trend continues, India's share of global steel, cement & power usage is likely to keep rising. Higher material intensity today is often a precursor to higher economic output tomorrow.

Maybe the better way to describe India isn't "consumption economy." It's a country simultaneously consuming, uplifting millions & building future productive capacity. 
India need a balancing act of Building future and taking care of the needy, which it is working towards

De-Dollarization lets peek into central bank reserves

Central banks are diversifying but US$ isn't giving up the throne anytime soon. Headlines scream de-dollarization bt US$ still makes up ~57% of global FX reserves. That's down from decades ago, but still miles ahead of everyone else.

Euro is the 2nd largest reserve currency at ~20%. But Europe faces weak growth, aging demographics, fiscal stress & fragmented politics. Hence no comfort for people looking to diversify away from US$

Then its China. Despite its economic size, RMB is only ~2% of global reserves & ~2% of global payments. Clear reflection of trust issues with the dragon. deep capital markets, convertibility & rule of law issues also there

They're moving into something with no issuer at all: Gold. Central banks themselves are now one of the biggest sources of gold demand globally, roughly buy ~30% of annual global mine production

Gold isn't rising only because investors are bullish. Significant chunk of global prodn is locked away by sovereign balance sheets. In 2026, central banks gold buying at slower pace vs 2025 due to 60% price rise.

Among the Major buyers were Poland, China, Brazil, India etc. 
Then there are few sellers too. Turkey has been among the largest sellers this year, reportedly selling ~83t YTD to support liquidity & FX/US$ needs.

That’s the problem. Though world want to move away from US$ in the long term but  issue in the medium term created due to lack of US$ in the country. 
Case in point Turkiye

Russia has also been a notable seller, reducing reserves by ~44t YTD as it seeks hard-currency liquidity. But Russia is also large producer of Gold

Gold is becoming a reserve diversification asset in a world where trust in fiat issuers is fragmenting.
BUT de-dollarization in reserves doesn't mean de-dollarization in trade.
That’s two very different thing

Global trade still run on the USD infrastructure. That network effect is incredibly hard to replace.
So its two-step process. Trade continues in USD.
But exporting nations convert a portion of their accumulated surplus reserves into gold, commodities, sovereign funds or other reserve assets.

The world may keep transacting in dollars while increasingly choosing not to store all its savings in dollars.

Conclusion:
Real story is different from "the end of the USD."
Reserve diversification is real.
Dollar replacement is not. Not in near future
